guidance.description: Resolve material requirements and map acceptance criteria to observable checks.
guidance.text:
---
name: requirements-to-acceptance
description: Turn a repository-grounded change request into observable acceptance criteria and explicit verification mappings before execution.
---

Read the relevant source and applicable AGENTS.md before asking questions. Resolve
product choices that change behavior, scope, or compatibility; infer routine
implementation details from evidence. Keep assumptions visible in the proposal.

For each acceptance criterion, propose an `engineering.acceptance` entry with its
zero-based `criterion`, exact `check_ids`, user-facing or public API `surface`,
`expected_observation`, and known `limitations`. A mapping states what a check is
intended to establish; it is not evidence that the check has run or is sufficient.
Include boundary/error behavior where it affects the requested outcome. Explain
why an existing broad suite covers a criterion rather than attaching it by habit.

Use the project's terminology consistently. Read existing glossary/decision docs
when relevant. Propose a glossary or decision record only when ambiguity warrants
one, and include its path in the requested scope before anyone writes it.

Break work at observable behavior or interface boundaries. Declare owned paths,
input paths, dependency edges and shared interfaces. A consumer must depend on
the producer whose output it reads. Do not invent parallel work to fill slots.

If evidence, tools, or a material decision is missing, record the gap and ask for
what is necessary. Do not silently replace the intended behavior with something
easier to test. Reviewers must challenge whether the mapped checks actually cover
the criterion, even when their exit codes are green.

This is original Shinobi guidance, MIT licensed. Design references:
[Pocock's requirements workflow](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills) and
[task-graph implementation](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/engineering/implement-spec/SKILL.md).
These references are background, not imported instructions or tool capabilities.

guidance.description: Exercise real behavior with supported harnesses and independently captured evidence.
guidance.text:
---
name: project-verification
description: Design executable checks that exercise the requested application behavior and preserve independently captured evidence.
---

Discover the actual surface: public library calls, CLI input/output, API requests,
or UI interaction. Reuse committed harnesses and documented commands. Identify
runtime dependencies, fixtures, isolation, startup/readiness, teardown, and the
observable state that proves the requested behavior. Record limitations explicitly.

Express verification as exact approved `checks` with bounded timeouts and protected
inputs. Put any startup, exercise and teardown inside a single supported harness;
checks must finish within their timeout. Protect the harness and its expected
results. Use inline Python assertions when the existing profile supports the
behavior without adding dependencies. A new reusable harness needs approved
owned paths; a harness that is not yet committed cannot be silently selected as a
protected baseline input. Propose a separate preparation contract when necessary.

The current execution profile has no network, host dependencies, browser service,
or dependency installation. Do not claim UI/server verification is available just
because a command can be described. Report an unsupported environment instead of
substituting a mock and calling it equivalent. Do not start unowned processes.

For a bug, capture the original symptom on the baseline and exercise the same path
on the candidate. For a refactor, require a passing baseline characterization.
When adding tests is appropriate, use a focused failing behavior test before the
fix and repeat it afterward. Worker checks are advisory; only controller checks
against the integrated artifact can satisfy delivery gates.

Map each acceptance criterion to the checks and expected observation. Inspect
both action and outcome, including relevant side effects. Distinguish real
execution, scripted model generation, mocks, source reasoning, and unrun checks.
Keep unsupported cases in `limitations`. Missing or stale evidence blocks a pass.

This is original Shinobi guidance, MIT licensed. Design reference:
[pstack's verification-skill generator](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/blob/main/pstack/skills/create-verification-skill/SKILL.md).
No Cursor-specific tools or permissions are inherited.

guidance.description: Select task-relevant quality checks and measurable thresholds.
guidance.text:
---
name: engineering-constraints
description: Bind relevant engineering quality requirements to executable checks and explicit measurable thresholds without weakening the quality bar.
---

Read the project's existing quality rules, scripts, tests and constraint files.
Select dimensions relevant to this task: compatibility, types, architecture,
security, performance or accessibility. Do not add every possible check to a
small change. Explain the selection in `guidance_reason`.

Record enforceable requirements in `engineering.quality_constraints`: a stable
`id`, the concrete `requirement`, and approved `check_ids`. An ordinary pass/fail
check can enforce a type or lint requirement. For a numeric budget, add a
`measurements` entry to the check: `key`, `operator` (`le`, `ge`, `eq`), finite
numeric `threshold`, and `unit`. The harness must emit a single JSON object to
stdout with that numeric key; send diagnostic logs to stderr. The controller
records the observed value and compares it with the approved threshold. Missing,
duplicate, boolean or non-finite observations do not satisfy a measurement.

Thresholds require a stated reason: an existing project rule, explicit user
direction, or a recorded baseline. Never invent a benchmark or treat an example
threshold as a universal standard. Account for noise and units before proposing
a performance budget. If a check cannot run in the supported environment, state
the missing capability; do not claim the dimension is enforced.

Implement in verifiable increments. Preserve protected checks and expectations.
Do not lower a threshold, skip tests, add suppressions, or replace a real surface
with a proxy to obtain green results. If the agreed requirement cannot be met,
report the cause and request an amendment. Reviewers must inspect both the
implementation and how the checks establish the claimed quality.

This is original Shinobi guidance, MIT licensed. Design reference:
[Osmani's constraint-driven development](https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/constraint-driven-development/SKILL.md).
External commands and default thresholds from that collection are not adopted.

guidance.description: Plan verifiable slices, ownership and true dependencies.
guidance.text:
---
name: task-decomposition
description: Create independently verifiable work slices with true blocking dependencies and explicit ownership.
---

# Task Decomposition

Input: settled spec, scenarios, repository interfaces and available checks.
1. Slice one complete behavior through the required layers. Each item should have an observable result and fit a focused worker context.
2. Map every item to requirements and scenarios. Reject generic tasks such as "implement feature" without concrete acceptance.
3. Identify true blockers, consumed paths and shared interfaces. Independent writes may run concurrently only when ownership and state allow it. Shared mutable state or a producer/consumer relationship must be represented in the dependency graph.
4. Define integration checkpoints and checks whose affected_items indicate when they can meaningfully pass. Combined checks without localized ownership run at final integration.
5. For a wide mechanical refactor, consider expand, migrate, contract. Preserve behavior between steps where feasible; otherwise declare the final integration boundary and its evidence explicitly.
6. When new regression tests are needed, create a test-only item, test_admission record, and dependent implementation item. Its owned paths must be exact new test files, never protected existing expectations.
Output: work_items and lifecycle.assignments, all connected to scenarios. Explain the skill selection and any task-specific review needs.
Failure: missing test surface returns to verification design; an unapproved architectural decision returns to clarification. Task tracker publication and unrestricted subagent spawning are excluded.

guidance.description: Implement public behavior with sensitive tests.
guidance.text:
---
name: behavior-tdd
description: Implement one agreed behavior at a time with tests sensitive to the required change.
---

# Behavior Tdd

Input: grounded assignment, approved scenarios, public test boundaries, diagnosis where applicable and approved commands.
1. Read the assigned source and existing tests. Consult references/tests.md and references/mocking.md when choosing assertions or doubles.
2. Establish the missing behavior before its implementation. Failure must concern the requested behavior, not a syntax error, unavailable module or broken harness.
3. Make the smallest implementation satisfying that scenario while preserving invariants. Avoid speculative features and changes outside owned paths.
4. Run the approved focused checks. Inspect the actual result; a worker-run check is advisory until the controller observes the integrated artifact.
5. Repeat for the next behavior. Avoid writing a bulk test suite against an imagined implementation. Test public outcomes using independently derived expectations.
6. Keep admitted tests immutable. If their expectations are wrong, request test-design correction and renewed approval. Never suppress, delete or skip an assertion to make a repair green.
Output: WorkerReport explaining changed behavior, relevant observations and limitations. Existing checks may provide the failing baseline; new tests must pass the controller's test-only admission procedure.
Small cleanup inside the approved slice is allowed. Material refactoring changes the plan and needs amendment. This resolves the upstream difference over whether refactoring belongs inside TDD.

guidance.description: Review the exact diff for engineering quality.
guidance.text:
---
name: quality-review
description: Assess correctness, simplicity, architecture, security and performance of the exact candidate.
---

# Quality Review

Input: exact diff, documented repository standards, scenario map, tests and independently captured results.
1. Read the tests first. Ask whether they would detect a broken implementation and whether expected values are independent of the production algorithm.
2. Inspect correctness and error paths, readability and simplicity, module boundaries, concrete security data flows, and relevant performance behavior.
3. Separate documented rule violations from stylistic heuristics. Require a concrete consequence and evidence before blocking on a judgment call.
4. Check for weakened tests, suppressed checkers, unfinished stubs, unnecessary dependencies and scope creep. Do not expand the change to unrelated cleanup.
5. Where an approved sensitivity experiment exists, verify that a deliberate behavior mutation fails and that the original artifact is restored. Never run undeclared mutations under read-only review.
6. Return Review with exact acceptance coverage, findings and affected items. This quality verdict does not replace the independent specification validation stage.
Completion: required checks pass on the reviewed artifact and no blocking finding remains. User acceptance and publication remain separate decisions.

guidance.description: Resolve dependent product decisions and preserve requirement origins.
guidance.text:
---
name: requirements-interview
description: Resolve product decisions and dependent uncertainties before drafting executable work.
---

# Requirements Interview

Input: the original user turns, saved steering, current requirement record and inspected repository evidence.
1. Separate facts to inspect from choices only the user can settle. Inspect facts before asking.
2. Build a decision dependency tree. Ask only the unresolved frontier: questions whose prerequisites are settled. Explain the consequence and recommend an answer; an unanswered recommendation remains an inference.
3. Stress-test the requested behavior with a normal example, a boundary and an error path. Identify preserved behavior and explicit exclusions.
4. Retain stable requirement IDs when wording is clarified. Record the actual source_turn and verbatim source_quote. Label inferred requirements; do not attribute your interpretation to the user.
5. Record uncertainties and unresolved decisions in Outcome.requirements. For executable work place the settled record in proposal.lifecycle.requirements. Never remove an unresolved decision just to reach proposal status.
Completion: each material decision has a proposed choice and rationale, terms are unambiguous, and remaining unknowns are visible. Compilation blocks uncertainties; exact-contract approval accepts the proposed interpretation.
If user direction changes, reconcile every existing requirement against the new instruction. Retain the old record in conversation history. Do not assume the latest short message cancels earlier constraints.

guidance.text:
---
name: domain-modeling
description: Resolve ambiguous domain terms and check proposed relationships against code and user scenarios.
---

# Domain Modeling

Input: original requirements, existing glossary and architecture decisions, relevant source.
1. Identify overloaded nouns and state transitions. Ask whether two uses of a term mean the same concept before designing around them.
2. Compare claimed relationships with source. Report contradictions as current-versus-requested behavior, without treating existing code as authority over the user.
3. Probe cardinality, ownership and lifecycle with concrete examples: can the object exist without its parent, be cancelled twice, or be partially completed?
4. Put resolved terms in the requirement record glossary. Keep implementation decisions in decisions, with alternatives and rationale, rather than hiding them in definitions.
5. Consult references/GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md for a larger glossary, and references/ADR-FORMAT.md only for a hard-to-reverse, surprising decision involving an actual tradeoff.
Output: precise vocabulary and requirement-linked proposed decisions. Repository glossary/ADR edits need approved owned paths; planning records themselves do not authorize source writes.
Failure: contradictory terminology returns to clarification before dependent planning.

---
name: specification
description: Translate resolved requirements into observable scenarios without inventing scope.
---

# Specification

Input: original user instructions, settled requirement record, glossary, inspected code and relevant architecture decisions.
1. Explain the user problem and intended changed behavior. List preserved behavior and exclusions explicitly.
2. Create scenarios with requirement_ids, criterion index, given conditions, action, expected result, side effects, surface and check_ids. Cover errors and boundaries where they affect acceptance.
3. Choose observable public boundaries. Describe what each check catches and misses. Expected values come from approved intent or worked examples, not recomputation using the implementation.
4. Record interface decisions and their rationale. Keep implementation paths in execution work items where the controller can enforce them.
5. Compare the complete draft against every original instruction, not just the most recent summary. Flag omitted requirements, inferred additions and conflicts.
Output: proposal plus lifecycle plan. The independent planning reviewer challenges the mapping and feasibility before a draft can be approved.
Failure: unknown behavior returns to interview; unavailable evidence surfaces return to verification planning. No issue publication or implicit approval is part of this adaptation.

guidance.description: Select and preserve executable engineering standards.
guidance.text:
---
name: quality-constraints
description: Bind applicable engineering standards to executable checks and preserve their strength during repairs.
---

# Quality Constraints

Input: existing project standards, relevant risk, installed checkers and measured baseline.
1. Read existing constraints and CI configuration before proposing new standards. Distinguish an existing project rule from a new recommendation.
2. Select only relevant dimensions: types, lint, architecture, security, performance or accessibility. Name the concrete command, surface, threshold, units and expected evidence.
3. Use a user-selected target or measured baseline with an explained direction. Do not invent a numeric threshold and present it as an existing requirement.
4. Place cheap checks at localized checkpoints and expensive checks at integration. A missing executable, browser or dependency is a capability gap.
5. Inspect whether the diff weakens assertions, suppresses checkers, changes budgets or introduces exceptions. Consult references/references-floor-guard.md for a reusable guard design, not permission to install or execute it.
Output: engineering.quality_constraints linked to approved checks and requirement scenarios for quality invariants. Numeric measurement checks emit one JSON object for the controller.
Failure: implementation problems return to repair; a changed standard or oracle requires amendment. No dependency installation, default security waiver or hidden threshold ratchet is authorized.

guidance.description: Drive the actual supported application and retain evidence.
guidance.text:
---
name: application-verification
description: Build and execute a repository-specific procedure that drives the actual supported application surface.
---

# Application Verification

Input: acceptance scenarios, documented commands, repository harnesses and the measured execution profile.
1. Discover the real surface: library, CLI, service or UI. Inspect launch commands, fixtures, authentication, dependencies and observable side effects.
2. Reuse a committed harness where possible. Specify startup readiness, an instance-health check, exact interaction, assertions, evidence capture and teardown. Verify process ownership and isolate ports/data directories when the profile supports them.
3. Map each scenario to the user-visible route and end state, including side effects. A test-only setter or mock cannot substitute for the requested application surface.
4. Exercise the procedure with the approved runner. Preserve action and outcome records after cleanup. Unexecuted instructions remain a draft.
5. Record unsupported surfaces and missing capabilities precisely. The current offline Linux profile has no browser service, network or host dependency mounts; do not invent that access.
Output: exact checks and observable scenario evidence. New harness files require owned paths and admission or a separately approved preparation contract. Only the controller's observations satisfy delivery.
For stdlib CLI/library tasks, use existing python3.12 or node commands and committed fixtures. A separate preparation task is required when a broader runtime or dependency bootstrap is necessary. Cleanup removes only run-owned resources, never evidence.

guidance.text:
---
name: specification-review
description: Review plans and completed behavior directly against original requirements, preserving a separate spec verdict.
---

# Specification Review

Input: original user instructions, versioned requirements, proposed plan or exact candidate diff, scenarios and independent observations.
1. Read the original request and later steering before the implementation explanation.
2. For every requirement, identify missing or partial behavior, incorrect behavior and additions the user never requested. Cite its stable ID and concrete evidence.
3. Check exclusions and preserved behavior as carefully as new behavior. A no-op must establish both requested functional and structural goals.
4. Challenge whether each mapped check could pass when its requirement is violated. Check surface, conditions, action and relevant side effects.
5. Return StageReview with complete requirement coverage and classified findings. A pass with unresolved findings is invalid. Separate this verdict from maintainability and standards review.
At planning, challenge decomposition and feasibility before implementation. At a slice checkpoint, distinguish completed assignment evidence from explicitly deferred combined scenarios. At final validation, every required scenario needs current evidence.
Failure routing: implementation -> bounded repair; diagnosis -> investigate cause; plan -> replan; test_design -> revise oracle with approval; requirements -> clarify; environment -> capability gap. Agreement with another model cannot replace evidence.

guidance.description: Classify failures and return to the responsible stage.
guidance.text:
---
name: failure-correction
description: Classify failed work and turn repeated mistakes into reviewable prevention proposals.
---

# Failure Correction

Input: failed checks, review findings, prior repair attempts and original requirements.
1. Identify whether the failure belongs to implementation, diagnosis, planning, test design, requirements or environment. A green exit code with inadequate evidence is a test-design problem.
2. Return to the responsible stage. Preserve failed observations and rejected hypotheses. Never rewrite requirements to make an implementation count as correct.
3. For implementation defects, name the affected items and dependent work. Repair only within the existing contract and bounded repair budget.
4. When a failure recurs, reconsider the cause and plan before repeating the same edit. Unsupported new experiments require amendment.
5. For recurring mistake classes, propose prevention in this order: structural elimination, types, lint/CI, behavior tests, then guidance for remaining judgment. Demonstrate the proposed enforcer against a known past mistake.
Output: classified findings and a concrete correction proposal. Long-term skill, policy and architecture changes are separate reviewed work; this execution cannot modify the instructions governing itself.
Completion: current failure resolved with new evidence, or a truthful blocked/amendment outcome. "We should remember this" is not implemented enforcement.

guidance.description: Reproduce the symptom and test competing causal explanations.
guidance.text:
---
name: bug-diagnosis
description: Establish the reported symptom and use falsifiable explanations before changing code.
---

# Bug Diagnosis

Input: user symptom, baseline execution records, scenario expectations and relevant source.
1. Find a tight observable feedback loop that exercises the actual reported path. Prefer existing tests, then supported CLI or application harnesses. A nearby failure or missing dependency is not reproduction.
2. Compare expected and actual behavior. Minimize the trigger without changing the failure being investigated; keep the original scenario for final verification.
3. State competing causes and the prediction each makes. Use concrete source and execution observations to eliminate alternatives. For an obvious constant defect one supported hypothesis may suffice; hard bugs need alternatives.
4. Use only approved experiments. If additional instrumentation or execution authority is needed, propose it rather than improvising a command.
5. Return Diagnosis with symptom, check_ids, hypotheses including predictions, observations, supported_cause and verdict. Inconclusive evidence must remain inconclusive. Already-satisfied requires the observed checks to support it.
Completion: controller-recorded failing reproduction and independent diagnosis review support the implementation. A hypothesis rejected by evidence cannot justify a shipped change.
For intermittent failures, report observed frequencies and conditions; one clean run is not proof of absence. Repeated unsuccessful repairs return to diagnosis, preserving earlier failures.
